title: Prime Spirals and Dirichlet's Theorem
hook: Opens by showing a visually stunning and mysterious spiral pattern of primes in polar coordinates — galaxies and rays with unexplained gaps — before revealing the puzzle.

scenes.purpose: Establish the surprising visual mystery to be explained

on_screen.desc: prime spiral in polar coordinates zooming out to reveal galaxy arms and straight rays
implicit question: what is going on here?

scenes.transition: spiral appears, then zooms out twice to reveal two distinct patterns
scenes.narration_gist: Plotting primes (p, p) in polar coordinates produces eerie galactic spirals and then straight rays with mysterious gaps — what's happening?

scenes.purpose: Give viewers the coordinate system vocabulary needed to understand the diagram

on_screen.desc: polar grid with a movable point, r-line, and arc
coordinate label (r, θ) with color-coded r and θ
arc sweeping to show θ in radians

scenes.transition: polar grid fades in over Cartesian plane; xy labels replaced by r and θ labels
scenes.narration_gist: A quick refresher: polar coordinates use radius r and angle θ in radians, where π is a half-turn and 2π is full circle.

scenes.purpose: Show what the (n, n) plot looks like for all whole numbers before restricting to primes

on_screen.desc: dots for n=1 through ~25 with coordinate labels (n, n)
Archimedean spiral tracing through the dots
r-line and arc animating one radian tick per step

scenes.transition: labeled dots appear one by one; spiral drawn through them; then non-primes fade to reveal prime-only subset
scenes.narration_gist: Plotting (n, n) for all integers creates an Archimedean spiral; each step rotates one radian and steps one unit outward.

scenes.purpose: Explain the small-scale 6-spiral structure and introduce residue class terminology

on_screen.desc: six color-coded spiral arms from multiples of 6 and offsets
formula 6k + r for r = 0..5 cycling
box: 'Residue classes mod 6' with plain-English gloss

scenes.transition: zoom back in from large scale; six arms highlighted one at a time cycling r value in formula
scenes.narration_gist: Six radians is just under 2π, so every six steps nearly completes a full turn, producing six spiral arms — each is a residue class mod 6.

scenes.purpose: Explain the 44-spiral scale via the 22/7 ≈ π rational approximation

on_screen.desc: 44 spiral arms for all whole numbers zoomed to medium scale
arithmetic box: 44 / 2π ≈ 7, so 44/7 ≈ 2π, so 22/7 ≈ π
residue classes mod 44 label

scenes.transition: zoom out from 6-spiral scale; whole-number spiral shown; 44 arms counted with click sounds
scenes.narration_gist: Taking 44 steps nearly completes 7 full turns because 44/7 ≈ 2π — the famous 22/7 approximation — producing 44 spiral arms as residue classes mod 44.

scenes.purpose: Reveal that spirals come from rational approximations to 2π, not from primes — deflating the mystical premise

on_screen.desc: whole-number spiral with 44 arms (clean)
prime-only spiral with 20 arms (gapped)
two separate questions: 'where do spirals come from?' vs 'what happens filtering to primes?'

scenes.transition: split screen introduced; cross drawn over original 'primes cause spirals' question
scenes.narration_gist: The spirals exist for ALL integers, not just primes — the mystery splits into two independent questions, one about rational approximations and one about prime distribution.

scenes.purpose: Explain which residue classes mod 44 survive when filtering to primes, using coprimality

on_screen.desc: 44 colored spiral arms with even and divisible-by-11 arms fading out
φ(44) = 20 with Euler's totient function label
'coprime / relatively prime' definition box

scenes.transition: arms eliminated one category at a time (evens, then multiples of 11); remaining 20 arms highlighted
scenes.narration_gist: Primes can only appear in residue classes coprime to 44 — exactly φ(44) = 20 of them — explaining the 20 visible spiral arms.

scenes.purpose: Resolve the 280-ray pattern via the even better approximation 355/113 ≈ π (mod 710)

on_screen.desc: nearly-straight rays at large zoom corresponding to residue classes mod 710
φ(710) = 280 derivation, factors 2, 5, 71

scenes.transition: large zoom out; rays highlighted in clumps of 4 with occasional missing tooth explained by factor 71
scenes.narration_gist: 710 steps nearly completes 113 full turns because 355/113 is an extraordinarily good π approximation, giving 710 nearly-straight ray classes of which φ(710) = 280 can contain primes.

scenes.purpose: Introduce Dirichlet's theorem: primes distribute evenly across all allowable residue classes

on_screen.desc: histogram bars showing prime counts per residue class mod 10 then mod 44, converging to equal heights
Dirichlet's theorem: fraction of primes with r mod n → 1/φ(n)
'Dirichlet's theorem' label

scenes.transition: histogram replaces spiral diagram; bars animate as more primes are counted, leveling off
scenes.narration_gist: The deep payoff: Dirichlet's theorem (1837) proves primes split equally among all coprime residue classes — a hard fact proven via complex analysis.

scenes.purpose: Zoom out meta-lesson: playful exploration of arbitrary data can lead to deep mathematics

on_screen.desc: reflective closing monologue text (no diagram)

scenes.transition: all visuals removed; narration only with sparse text
scenes.narration_gist: The polar plot of primes was arbitrary and unimportant, but following its questions leads to Dirichlet's theorem — and rediscovering ideas yourself makes them stick as familiar friends.

lessons: Open with the most visually surprising output first, then work backwards to explain it — earn attention before demanding comprehension.
Split a compound mystery into explicit sub-questions on screen so the audience always knows which thread is currently being answered.
Use a zoom animation as a narrative device: each zoom level reveals a new layer of the pattern and triggers the next explanatory beat.
Introduce jargon only after the viewer has already understood the concept intuitively — then frame the term as a compact label for something familiar.
When deflating a false premise, show the corrected version side-by-side with the original so the distinction is spatial, not just verbal.
Use live-updating histograms or counters to let abstract theorems reveal themselves empirically before stating them formally.
